## What are we doing when we do social science?

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is not private. It is offered to others so they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
That handover is the whole enterprise. Everything today is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
Start with the obvious question that nobody asks out loud. What are we actually doing? We are making claims about the world – claims that could turn out to be wrong, and that come with some statement of how we would find out. And a claim is not a private possession. You publish it so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it, and build on top of it. That handover is the entire enterprise. A finding nobody else can examine is not a contribution, it is an assertion. So when we ask today whether social science is in trouble, the question is really quite specific: does the handover work? Can someone else pick your finding up and do anything with it?
:::

## Three arguments that made people nervous {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments, in order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis in 2005 made the theoretical case: put together small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and lots of teams chasing the same question, and you can show that most published findings in a field will be false without anybody breaking a single rule. Then Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn demonstrated it in practice – give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have, and you can push a five per cent false-positive rate above sixty. They proved it by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes you younger. And Gelman and Loken added the subtlety that I find hardest to shake: you do not have to run many tests for this to bite. If the one test you ran was chosen after you looked at the data, its p-value is already wrong.
:::

## And then people counted {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology experiments**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields, different designs, and in both **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes
And then people stopped arguing and counted. The Open Science Collaboration took a hundred psychology experiments and replicated them properly – high power, original materials, the original authors consulted where possible. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result. Thirty-six per cent of the replications did, and the effect sizes came back at about half the original size. That is the study that made 'replication crisis' a phrase outside methodology seminars. The second one is closest to home, because it is ours: seventy-three teams of sociologists and political scientists, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign, let alone the significance. Different fields, different designs, and the same uncomfortable conclusion. The finding depends on the finder.
:::

## It is not mostly fraud {.smaller}

::: {.small}
The mechanism is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these practices – not fraud, the ordinary kind [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person. That is exactly why the problem is hard: you cannot fix it by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
Now the important qualification, and I want to be emphatic about it. This is not mostly a story about fraud. Fraud exists and it is spectacular when it surfaces, but it is rare and it is not what these numbers are measuring. The mechanism is ordinary and it is structural. Journals want novel, clean, significant results, so that is what gets submitted. Every analysis contains dozens of small, individually defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data, because how else would you make them. Nobody writes up the twelve specifications that did not work, so the reader sees one path through a garden with hundreds. And in most cases neither the data nor the code are available, so nobody can check any of it. John, Loewenstein and Prelec went and asked researchers directly, anonymously, with a mechanism designed to make truthful answers worth giving – and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. Not one of those steps requires a bad actor. Which is exactly why the problem is hard: you cannot solve it by hiring better people. [pause] So suppose you did hire the best people you could find, gave them all the same data and the same question, and watched. Somebody did exactly that.
:::

## Twenty-nine teams, one question {.smaller}

::: {.small}
**The question.** Are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones?

**The data.** One dataset, sent to everyone: 2,053 players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the 3,147 referees they played under, and **146,028 player–referee pairs**. Skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who did not know the research question.

**The design.** Twenty-nine teams analysed it independently. They reviewed each other's approaches *before* anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the first many-analysts study. Every one since is a variation on it – including the one you are inside today.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne
:::

::: notes
So let me show you the study that started all of this, because everything after it, including our own day, is a variation on its design. Silberzahn and colleagues, twenty eighteen. The question is deliberately concrete: are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones? The data went to everyone identically – two thousand and fifty-three players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the three thousand referees they had played under, and a hundred and forty-six thousand player-referee pairs, with skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who were not told the research question. And then the part that makes it a study rather than a survey: twenty-nine teams analysed it independently, reviewed each other's approaches before anybody had seen a single result, revised, and only then compared answers. Nobody could tune their method to get a number they liked, because nobody knew what number anyone was getting.
:::

## All twenty-nine, side by side

```{r}
#| label: silberzahn-forest
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 5.0
# The paper's Figure 3, rebuilt from the authors' published values rather than
# reproduced as an image: every team, every interval, grouped by the response
# distribution it assumed. Colour is ours – the original is monochrome – and
# marks whether the interval excludes 1. Teams 21 and 27 have intervals running
# to 11.5 and 78.7; the published figure truncates both and asterisks them, and
# so does this.
CLIP <- 3.2
szf <- silberzahn29 |>
  mutate(hi_draw = pmin(or_hi, CLIP),
         lab = paste0(team, ". ", tidy_approach(approach))) |>
  arrange(distribution, or) |>
  mutate(lab = factor(lab, levels = rev(lab)))

ggplot(szf, aes(or, lab, colour = significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "longdash", colour = grey_mid) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = or_lo, xmax = hi_draw), height = 0, linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(data = filter(szf, or_hi > CLIP), aes(x = CLIP + 0.04, label = "*"),
            size = 5, vjust = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ncl_blue, `FALSE` = d_red),
                      breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL,
                      labels = c("interval excludes 1", "interval includes 1")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.03))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.42, CLIP + 0.1)) +
  facet_grid(distribution ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = "odds ratio", y = NULL,
       caption = paste("Above 1: dark-skinned players red-carded more often.",
                       "* interval runs past the edge (teams 21 and 27).")) +
  theme_slide(11) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 1, colour = "grey45", size = 9,
                                    margin = margin(t = 4)),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "right",
        legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -6, 0),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey25"),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey92"),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold",
                                         colour = ncl_blue, hjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = element_text(colour = "grey25", hjust = 0, size = 8.5),
        panel.spacing.y = unit(0.45, "lines"))
```

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne, Figure 3, rebuilt from the published values at osf.io/gvm2z.
:::

::: notes
And here is what came back. Read it as a list of twenty-nine analyses of one dataset. The odds ratios run from nought point eight nine to two point nine three – the low end says dark-skinned players were red-carded slightly *less* often – and the median is one point three one. Twenty of the twenty-nine intervals exclude one; nine do not. So about two thirds found an effect and a third did not, on identical data. [pause] Now look at the left column, because that is where the day's real subject is. The teams are grouped by the response distribution they assumed – linear, logistic, Poisson, and two that fit none of the three. That is not a detail of implementation. It is a decision each team made, defensibly, before touching the data, and it is the same kind of decision you will be making after lunch. Hold on to that grouping; we come back to it twice.
:::

## 'Replication' crises

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Another 'replication' crisis – terminological confusion?
:::
::: {.fragment}
The term 'reproducibility' has been used as a synonym for a number of different characteristics – reproducibility, robustness, replicability, repeatability, credibility, and trustworthiness.
:::
[[Successfully rerun the same code on the same data?]{colour="#b22222"}]{.fragment}
[[Re-analyse the same data a different way?]{colour="#1C69A8"}]{.fragment}
[[Collect fresh data and analyse it in the same way?]{colour="#4D179A"}]{.fragment}
[[Using the same data and same analysis but asking a different question?]{colour="#3C6301"}]{.fragment}
[[Asking the same question but answering it with fresh data and a different analysis?]{colour="#3BB8DB"}]{.fragment}
::::

::: notes
So: twenty-nine competent teams, one dataset, and no agreement. Now notice what I have carefully not said yet – what *kind* of failure that is. And that turns out to be the whole difficulty, because part of the problem is the word itself. For years 'replication' covered everything: rerunning someone's code, re-analysing their data a different way, collecting new data altogether. Those are three different operations, answering three different questions – but because we called them all 'replication', the crisis debates had people talking past each other for a decade. So before any numbers, we need vocabulary.
:::
